title: Beijing Tightens Grip On Solar Exports: Will Trump Play America's Quartz Card?
desc:
Beijing Tightens Grip On Solar Exports: Will Trump Play America's Quartz Card?

Beijing's new restrictions on advanced solar technologies and equipment suggest the Trump-Xi meeting in Washington did little to ease trade tensions. The new measures aim to preserve China's technological advantage as the US and India expand domestic solar manufacturing. This reinforces ongoing concerns about critical materials, where Beijing has placed export controls on tungsten, germanium, gallium, and antimony.

Bloomberg cites a statement released by China's Ministry of Commerce earlier this morning announcing that it would add 12 solar-related technologies and core equipment to its export-control list, citing national security concerns. The changes form part of a broader revision covering 40 technologies, including AI and biopharmaceuticals.

"In recent years, the application of solar technology in sensitive fields such as aerospace, national defense, unmanned equipment, and high-security-level infrastructure has been continuously expanding," the ministry said in the statement.

The statement continued, "The national security risks that may be caused by the export of solar technology have been constantly rising. It is necessary to implement timely and appropriate supervision."

The measures include a ban on exports of production technology for perovskite and solar modules, advanced technologies that offer higher efficiency and potential use in space-based solar power. Restrictions will also apply to certain technologies used to produce polysilicon, a key solar-panel material.

According to BloombergNEF analysts, the new controls could complicate efforts to diversify the global solar supply chain. Manufacturers in the US and India still depend on China for some critical materials, equipment, and technologies.

The question now is how the Trump administration will respond, if it can.

Trump administration trade officials could restrict exports of US high-purity quartz to China through export controls and licensing requirements.

China's solar dominance remains vulnerable to restrictions on US-sourced high-purity quartz, giving Trump potential leverage.

title: For restaurants Covid-19 was a crisis – pandemic loans are proving a disaster
desc:
Low-interest loans kept many eateries afloat. But the industry never recovered enough for them to repay the debt

For almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021.

At the time, it provided a desperately needed lifeline. He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. But when his business didn’t recover, the disaster loan turned out to be a disaster of its own.

title: Will Trump’s economy sink Republicans in the US midterm elections? Our reporters answered your questions
desc:
The high cost of living has Americans angrier than ever. Guardian reporters answered your questions about the US economy ahead of November

  • Sign up for the Stakes newsletter for more midterms coverage

  • Send us your questions on Trump’s immigration agenda ahead of the midterms

LucccA asks: Why are labor unions in the US still not as well-organized compared to the rest of the world? I know there was a push against them in the past—does that still have an effect today? Also, why are there so many right-leaning unions in the US?

Michael: A lot of reasons. The US has low union density compared to other wealthy nations, currently at 10.0%, and that has been on a precipitous decline for the past few decades for a variety of reasons that include anti-union and union busting campaigns, outdated labor laws where employers often retaliate for union organizing or delay bargaining for years, as we are seeing with Starbucks, where there is no union contract after nearly five years since the first store won its union election in December 2021.Right to work laws in the US also undermine labor unions and starve them of resources. To the extent that there are right leaning labor unions in the US, they typically are law enforcement unions that consistently endorse and back Republican candidates despite the Republican Party in the US opposing collective bargaining. Some unions like the Teamsters have been making efforts to get Republicans to support legislation and in turn receive endorsements from the union, and this has shown up this election cycle with the Teamsters endorsing Republicans like Congressman Max Miller or Kansas Senator Roger Marshall, who are both facing very competitive re-election battles.

Heather: There’s a bunch of ideas floating around on cutting costs for groceries, healthcare and energy bills. A key thing Democrats are promising if they regain power in Congress is to wrestle back authority on trade and repeal Trump’s tariffs, which would lower what it costs compaines to import. A second is to advance a vote to stop the war in Iran, which could calm fuel prices. If Democrats retake the Senate, expect Elizabeth Warren to become chair of the powerful banking committe, and push forward some curbs on private equity investments. And Democrats have been coalescing around more government funding for childcare, a notable move to the left in recent years. Hakeem Jeffries, who will be House Speaker if Democrats win there, is promising to reinstate ACA tax cuts and roll back Medicaid cuts, but the party is divided on Medicare For All, with DSA candidates making promises on the campaign trail and more centrist Dems being pretty quiet.

Republicans running for Congress have been talking a lot about ways to lower gas prices, especially suspending the fuel tax, and shaving utility bills by making tech companies and other big users pay more. Some have promised to curb Trump’s tariffs, including Michigan’s Mike Rogers, and others are proposing suspending data center building after public backlash.

title: The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is coming | Larry Elliott
desc:
Finance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. There is little chance of that

Not much has gone right for the global economy this year, and plenty has gone wrong. Two big regional wars are destabilising prices and supply chains everywhere. Businesses and consumers are feeling the effects of a serious energy shock. Rising inflation has made it a lot more expensive for governments to finance their debts. China and the US are at loggerheads over trade.

Yet, so far, the impact has been modest. It is something of a miracle that the finance ministers and central bank governors gathered for this year’s annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok are not having to deal with a full-blown crisis. This is not like the autumn of 2008, when the meetings took place during the worst of the global banking meltdown.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

title: Britain Is Accelerating Towards Crisis
desc:
Britain Is Accelerating Towards Crisis

Authored by David Betz and Michael Rainsborough via The Daily Sceptic,

Something is going badly wrong across Western societies, and the sense of political dislocation is no longer a fringe concern. Trust in institutions has fallen, established political parties are losing support and arguments over immigration and national identity have become sharp dividing lines.

In Germany, the President now warns openly of a return to the political divisions of the Weimar era. In France, a protest movement that began in schools has spread across the country, bringing arson, mass arrests and violent clashes with riot police to cities from Strasbourg to Marseille. Across Europe, insurgent parties of Left and Right prosper on dissatisfaction with political systems that seem increasingly unable to correct themselves. Britain exhibits the same symptoms. The question is why governments confronted by such conditions so often appear to aggravate the problems rather than address their causes.

Aggravating the conditions driving the crisis follows the logic of accelerationism. Most closely associated with the British philosopher Nick Land, accelerationism holds that an existing order contains forces which, once unleashed, drive change forward and ultimately overwhelm attempts to restrain them. Rather than arrest the process, accelerationist thought embraces its intensification, although versions of the idea on Left and Right differ markedly over where it might lead. The essential rationale remains: if the existing order contains forces capable of destroying or transforming it, remove the restraints and let them run their course.

Judged by that standard, Britain's ruling classes are accelerationists par excellence. They oversee economic stagnation, mounting national debt, growing welfare dependency, the decay of town centres and public services, and deepening social divisions, compounded by rapid demographic change and repeated failures to deliver effective immigration controls. Their own reports document segregation, declining trust and failures of integration, yet governments refuse to change the policies contributing to those problems. As opposition becomes more organised and disruptive, the state responds with surveillance and speech restrictions, as well as two-tier policing and justice. Grievance produces resistance, resistance produces stronger enforcement, and stronger enforcement fuels the grievance.

We first raised the likelihood of Britain moving towards violent social breakdown in a short article 'The British Road to Dirty War' in January 2019. At that time the prognosis was seen as controversial, not least within our own university. We were 'cancelled' and removed from our positions of authority in the Department of War Studies for daring to raise this heretical possibility.

Now, the prospect is no longer confined to supposedly dissenting academics. In June 2026, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch warned that communal divisions risked taking Britain towards civil war. What was once been dismissed as an alarmist prediction was now being voiced by the leader of the opposition. Recognising the danger is one thing, though; reconsidering the policies contributing to the problem is quite another.

Governments are not spectators to the forces at work, which raises the most fundamental - and still largely unanswered - question in the civil war debate: why, despite endless warnings about growing social fracture and the prospect of civil strife, do Britain's ruling classes continue pursuing policies that exacerbate these tensions? Why persist on a course that threatens to unleash forces capable of sweeping away the very political order upon which their own survival depends?

Is it simply incompetence?

The current debate over immigration illustrates this paradox most clearly. So, let's begin from the obvious explanation: that it is all a case of ineptitude.

There is plenty of evidence of incompetence, but as an explanation for the failure to tackle the wider problems generated by unconstrained immigration, legal and illegal alike, it doesn't quite wash. For example, consecutive administrations have promised to reduce immigration but then consciously moved in the opposite direction. Brexit should have removed one familiar explanation for the inability to control national borders. Instead, the system introduced in 2021 widened access to overseas labour by lowering skills and salary thresholds, removing the cap on skilled workers and abolishing the resident labour market test. Net migration subsequently reached 944,000 in the year ending March 2023. The rules were later tightened, and the figures fell but remain historically high.

Nor can governments claim that the negative social consequences are a surprise. As far back as 2001, the Cantle Report after the riots in Bradford and Oldham described communities living "parallel lives". As Home Secretary, Theresa May warned in 2010 that poorly managed immigration placed pressure on public services and damaged community relations. David Cameron declared state multiculturalism a failure in 2011. The Casey Review reiterated many of these findings in 2016. In November 2024, the Government stated that its intent was to restore order to a "broken" immigration system. In 2025 Keir Starmer warned of Britain becoming an "island of strangers", while the Government's 2026 social cohesion plan acknowledges similar problems.

The recurrence of such warnings points towards more than poor judgement. Other forces are clearly at work. For example, large employers, notably in the health and social care sectors, have come to depend heavily upon international recruitment, giving them a powerful interest in maintaining existing arrangements, while the detrimental social impacts are borne by the population at large, including fiscal costs, pressure upon housing, infrastructure, health and welfare services, wage suppression and rising crime, especially in sexual offending.

These social costs did not have to be distributed in this way. Employers could have been encouraged to invest more heavily in domestic recruitment, training and retention. Such choices would have imposed burdens of their own, but political decisions necessarily involve trade-offs. Governments instead accommodated business demands for access to overseas labour while leaving the wider population, especially those on lower incomes and in already deprived areas, to bear the burden.

Over time, the logic acquired a momentum of its own. Dependence upon overseas labour was increasingly cited as a reason why immigration could not substantially be reduced. Policy created dependency; dependency became the argument for continuing the policy. Cue the inevitable smug Question Time audience member who bewails that without migrants, who will staff the NHS, and more importantly, who will serve us in Pret?

Incompetence alone cannot explain why governments pursue policies that heighten the danger of civil strife. Governments have certainly miscalculated, but they have also made deliberate choices, sustaining existing arrangements long after the resulting social tensions had been officially admitted.

Another failure, another report

Faced with declining social cohesion, governments have proved far readier to devise new administrative remedies than to reconsider the policies contributing to the problem. The latest example is Protecting What Matters, the Government's 2026 social cohesion plan. It acknowledges that large-scale migration makes community bonds harder to maintain, points to continuing segregation and records falling trust and worsening tensions.

Having diagnosed the problems, Whitehall proposes national integration standards, local cohesion plans, new mechanisms for detecting communal friction and a Social Cohesion Measurement Framework. After 25 years of reports documenting deepening societal divisions, the answer is apparently another programme for managing the consequences, while leaving the policies contributing to those divisions untouched. One set of policies creates the problems that justify another.

To illustrate the contradictory thinking at work, in March 2026 Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood accepted that people seeing illegal small-boat arrivals and the pace of immigration more generally had good reason to feel that matters were "out of control". Yet having conceded the failure of control, she turned to what she regarded as the more grievous threat: the growth of ethno-nationalism. Government policies, in other words, had provoked precisely the political reaction she now proposed to combat.

Combating the rise of the 'far-Right' gives government a new set of tasks. Anger over immigration is treated as a threat to social cohesion; hostility towards immigration becomes a potential source of extremism; communal tensions require monitoring and intervention. The policies generating much of the discontent stay in place, while government expands its efforts to contain the political reaction.

The accelerationist dynamic can therefore be summarised as a feedback loop. Policies that generate discontent are maintained; government seeks to contain the reaction they have caused; containment further exacerbates the grievance against the state. By treating the political expression of that grievance as a problem to be suppressed, the authorities intensify the very forces they are trying to control.

When political correction fails

Democratic politics depends upon the possibility of correction. Governments can be removed, policies reversed and lost arguments fought again at the next election. People can profoundly dislike a policy while accepting the political system, provided they retain confidence that democratic institutions offer a peaceful means of changing the direction of policy.

The scale and pace of recent immigration have tested that bargain. Governments of both major parties have promised greater control, yet policy has either barely changed or failed to deliver the promised results. The lesson is corrosive: when elections fail to translate public demands into political change, the appeal of seeking redress through other means inevitably grows.

Loss of faith in the capacity of elections to bring about meaningful change also extends to the institutions responsible for implementing government policy. The civil service, courts and police cease to appear as neutral instruments of democratic governance and come to be seen as obstacles to popular will, seemingly unresponsive to demands expressed through the ballot box.

Mismanaged immigration also accelerates the communalisation of politics. Competition over housing, schools and public resources, alongside disputes over cultural norms and practices, becomes organised increasingly around ethnic or religious identities. Government reinforces these divisions when it consults faith and community organisations, directs programmes towards particular groups and seeks representatives to speak on their behalf. A state that encourages minorities to consolidate politically along communal lines should hardly be surprised when the majority begins to do the same, and nativist demands follow.

If elections fail to change policy, while institutions meant to arbitrate political disputes are themselves seen as favouring competing communal interests, confidence that the system offers a peaceful route to political change begins to collapse. Opposition then moves beyond electoral politics. Protest becomes more confrontational, direct action more attractive and resistance easier to justify.

When containment becomes escalation

As opposition moves from protest to direct obstruction, the full weight of the state is brought to bear against those who resist. At Eastney Marina in Portsmouth, the authorities facilitated the landing and onward transport of migrants brought across the Channel by criminal smuggling networks, despite fierce local opposition. The determination to secure their passage stood in stark contrast to the refusal to reconsider the policies that had provoked the confrontation.

Such confrontations become tests of government authority: whether the state can enforce its decisions in the face of organised resistance. For those resisting, the same confrontation raises a question of legitimacy: whether governments that have consistently ignored demands for political change can still claim the obedience of their citizens.

Once resistance challenges the state's authority, changing course becomes politically more difficult than an earlier correction would have been. A policy reversal secured through ordinary politics can be defended on its merits; one made under pressure from direct action risks demonstrating that disruption works. The policy becomes a test of the government's resolve, giving ministers another reason to hold their ground.

For those resisting, the lesson is precisely the opposite, providing another reason to question the state's legitimacy. Elections, manifesto promises and official reviews have failed to deliver the promised reductions in immigration. Yet a government perceived as unwilling to secure the national borders proves ready to deploy its coercive powers against those challenging its decisions. The contrast reinforces the belief that open defiance is the only language the state appears to understand.

The two responses feed upon each other. Resistance gives government stronger reasons to assert its authority; the resulting enforcement deepens the grievances driving resistance. A classic escalatory dynamic develops, with each side supplying the other with reasons for its next move.

The confrontation over illegal Channel crossings thus develops into a more fundamental struggle over political power: whether change can still be secured through ordinary politics, or whether the outcome will increasingly be settled by force.

The self-preservation trap

As things deteriorate, the state is much better equipped to suppress a protest than to address its underlying causes. No comparable machinery springs into action when a policy fails for 20 years. Revising immigration policy requires ministers to confront organised interests, institutional dependencies and assumptions embedded across government. Arresting someone who blocks a port is considerably easier than reconsidering the policies that brought them there in the first place.

The grievances behind such protests have accumulated through years of political choices whose costs have been deferred, dispersed or transferred elsewhere. Some difficulties have arisen from governmental inaction; others are the direct result of policies deliberately pursued. Yet governments that have shown little inclination to address these problems become remarkably decisive when the resulting tensions threaten their authority. The authoritarian impulse asserts itself as those in power seek to defend the political order over which they preside.

Accidental accelerationists?

Accelerationism ordinarily implies intention. There is little reason to presume that Britain's ruling classes consciously seek the social upheaval or political destruction that accelerationist ideas envisage. Governments, however, are hardly innocent bystanders to the forces they help set in motion. They decide which interests to accommodate, determine which costs they are prepared to impose and follow the same course long after the dangers are plain to see. Absence of intention does not imply absence of responsibility.

Mass immigration and multiculturalism provide the clearest illustration. Neither simply happened to Britain. Both reflected political choices and, in some quarters, ideological convictions about diversity, national identity and the kind of society Britain ought to become. No democratic mandate was ever sought for so profound a transformation of British society.

The political and institutional interests sustaining mass immigration and multiculturalism also evolve over time. One government liberalises immigration for economic reasons; another preserves the system because public services have become dependent upon overseas recruitment; institutions built around multicultural policies acquire constituencies, practices and assumptions of their own. Later governments inherit both the policies and the costs of dismantling them. Choice becomes interest, interest hardens into dependency, and dependency is then presented as necessity.

Britain's present difficulties are therefore no mere accident. The policies contributing to them were consciously chosen, defended and sustained despite successive official warnings about their effects.

So, are they accelerationists?

Why, then, do Britain's ruling classes continue along a course that increases the danger of civil conflict? The answer lies in how the different forces we have examined combine to reinforce one another. Six propositions bring the argument together.

1. Incompetence explains part of the failure but cannot explain the refusal to change course. Governments make bad decisions, misjudge consequences and fail to deliver what they publicly promise. But such failings cannot adequately explain why, when the dangers have long been recognised, governments of both major parties nevertheless pursue much the same policies.

2. Powerful interests have a stake in maintaining the status quo. Employers and public services have become heavily dependent on overseas recruitment. Their interests are organised and well represented in government. Governments face stronger incentives to accommodate these organised interests than to address the consequences borne by the population at large.

3. Ideology shapes what governments are prepared to recognise and reconsider. Immigration and multiculturalism reflect convictions about diversity, national identity and the desirability of social transformation. Such beliefs influence which outcomes governments welcome, which difficulties they tolerate and which objections they regard as legitimate. Political commitments can survive mounting evidence that the resulting changes are generating serious divisions.

4. Political choices create institutional dependencies that make reversal progressively harder. Employers and public services organise staffing around overseas recruitment, while government builds institutions around the society its policies have helped create. Over time, decisions acquire powerful defenders and become embedded in administrative practice. Reversing these policies then requires governments to confront interests, assumptions and dependencies that their predecessors helped establish.

5. The failure of democratic correction encourages opposition beyond ordinary politics. Voters are promised greater control over national borders, but governments fail to deliver. Reports identify problems without resolving them; elections change governments without changing the direction of policy. As confidence in democratic redress weakens, resistance becomes more organised and disruptive. The failure to address grievances through established political channels creates the conditions in which more confrontational methods acquire greater appeal.

6. The defence of political authority can become a source of further escalation. Once resistance challenges the state's ability to enforce its decisions, changing course risks appearing to reward direct action and weaken formal authority. Governments therefore become more inclined to suppress opposition, even as the causes of discontent go unaddressed. Stronger enforcement, in turn, reinforces the conviction among opponents that the democratic process offers no effective remedy. The effort to preserve authority risks intensifying the confrontation that threatens its legitimacy.

So, are Britain's ruling classes the ultimate accelerationists? Not in the literal sense, of course. Accelerationism consciously embraces forces within an existing order whose intensification drives towards its destruction or transformation. Britain's ruling classes, one assumes, do not subscribe to any such doctrine. Yet their policies have set in motion a recognisably accelerationist dynamic. As elections repeatedly fail to produce the promised changes in policy, governments become more determined to assert their authority over those who resist. Governments unable to address the causes of political conflict prove considerably more capable of policing dissent. Suppressing resistance is easier, at least in the short term, than correcting the conditions that generate resistance.

Britain's ruling classes need not seek the destruction of the existing order. They need only defend it until self-preservation becomes self-destruction.

David Betz is Professor of War in the Modern World, King's College London. Michael Rainsborough is Professor of Strategic Theory and Director of the Centre for Future Defence and National Security, Canberra.

title: "Engineering Flex": Flying Tesla Roadster Wows Wall Street, But Production Waits Until 2028
desc:
"Engineering Flex": Flying Tesla Roadster Wows Wall Street, But Production Waits Until 2028

Tesla shares rose 4% in early New York premarket trading after Thursday night's flying Roadster reveal delivered what HSBC analysts called an "engineering flex." However, for reservation holders who have been waiting years, the "Back to the Future"-style sports car that can perform midair barrel rolls using SpaceX air thrusters came with another dose of reality: production won't begin until 2028.

Real life, baby https://t.co/3QEqn18wig

— Tesla (@Tesla) October 16, 2026

HSBC senior global autos analyst Michael Tyndall wrote early Friday morning his first take on last night's Tesla Roadster reveal, saying it was "an engineering flex rather than a demonstration of earnings power; still some wait for first deliveries."

Here's Tyndall first take:

Tesla revealed the Roadster at a SpaceX facility on 15 October, almost nine years after it started taking orders/deposits for the model in November 2017.

Financials - limited details

  • No details on financial impact of the model (i.e. indication of potential units or pricing, other than reservation amount on Tesla's website). The model is said to go into production in 2028. Global Mobility's latest forecast (released 15 October) does not include any production estimates for this model.
  • On Tesla's 1Q26 earnings call, CEO Musk had said that: "I don't think it [Roadster] moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint, but it is very cool".
  • Tesla has not disclosed how many total orders it has for the model so far since Nov-17. The Founders Series that required a USD250k deposit (limited to 1,000 units) was sold out (totalling USD250m in deposits) but there is no clarity on the orders for the Standard version for which Tesla collected USD50k deposits per unit.

Regulatory approvals - no clarity

InsideEVs (15 October) notes that during the reveal event CEO Musk was "cagey about whether it would actually be legal to drive on public roads". Tesla's reservation page for the model says:

  • The base "Performance" version is "road ready"
  • The Thrust augment (limited release) is "race ready" - so potentially cannot be used on public roads
  • The Rocket augment is not approved for public road use and not available in all regions

Key questions

  • How much of the technology will make it to the final vehicles? How much of it will pass type approval legislation?
  • Is 2028 production time-line realistic? Given the novel nature of the technology are we likely to see further delays?
  • Given the pivot away from human-driven cars, does this represent a worthwhile use of R&D expenditure?

Separately, JPMorgan analyst Rajat Gupta, who rates Tesla neutral, said the new Roadster's "rocket upgrade" showcases deep collaboration with SpaceX, though production remains years behind the original schedule.

"Production is targeted for 2028, compared with the original 2020 delivery target announced when the vehicle was first unveiled in 2017," Gupta said.

Notably, the flying Tesla Roadster appears to borrow technology from SpaceX, such as air thrusters, which supports the case that Tesla and SpaceX share not just materials but also engineering.

Barclays senior autos analyst Dan Levy wrote Thursday about the prospects of a Tesla-SpaceX merger, in which he said:

The possibility of a Tesla/SpaceX merger has increasingly become the consensus expectation, as widely highlighted by media reports. Even Elon Musk has publicly alluded to a combination: On the most recent Tesla earnings call, Elon Musk pointed to "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX, and in an interview at the All-In Summit last month, he noted, "With all this collaboration, on so many levels, who can imagine what action one might take when there's so much close collaboration in so many areas."

Levy expects a merger announcement ahead of Tesla's annual general shareholder meeting in December 2026.

title: "Perfectly-Integrated" African Migrant On Trial For Strangling, Dismembering His Wife
desc:
"Perfectly-Integrated" African Migrant On Trial For Strangling, Dismembering His Wife

Via Remix News

An African man, who was described as "perfectly integrated," is on trial in Bonn on charges connected to the strangling murder of his wife, whom he then dismembered. The woman's remains were later found in several locations across Germany, according to court proceedings.

Asmerom G., 42, an Eritrean national, faces the charges in Bonn Regional Court in North Rhine-Westphalia. The case stems from events in mid-November 2025 involving his wife, Weghata A., 32. The couple had married in Ethiopia in 2019, and she arrived in Germany in 2024 through family reunification.

The defendant allegedly met his wife, 32-year-old Weghata A., inside his car, where they began arguing on their way back from a church visit. According to Bonner Generalanzeiger newspaper, Asmerom G. later told police that his wife told him their 3-month-old girl was not his biological child. He reportedly could not remember what happened next.

According to prosecutors, Asmerom G. then strangled his wife in the back seat of the car in a parking lot in Bonn, directly in front of the baby who was sitting in a child seat.

After the crime, the defendant is said to have driven with the body and the baby in the car to the Monastery of Saint Anthony, 160 kilometers away, where he abandoned the little girl in the stroller when it was only 2 degrees Celsius (35 degrees Fahrenheit).

Fortunately for the girl, monks found the child just 40 minutes after she was dropped off.

Asmerom G. then went to work dismembering Weghata's body, including packing her hands and head in plastic bags.

He left the torso behind, which was found at the end of November 2025. Asmerom G. left the body parts on the side of the autobahn, on the A45. The head of the woman was discovered by garbage collectors in April 2026.

Asmerom G. was arrested in Ethiopia and extradited to Germany. He has a prior conviction for aggravated assault. On the first day of the trial, he declined to comment on the allegations. Defense attorney Martin Kretschmer has said the case rests largely on DNA evidence and mobile-phone data.

Kretschmer told Bild newspaper, "Until his arrest, he was considered perfectly integrated."

German media was even singing his praises in 2016. The man from Eritrea had landed a job as an electrical assistant at a firm in Rheinbach, in North Rhine-Westphalia, and gave interviews about leaving his homeland three years earlier to escape political persecution.

He wanted German citizenship, he said. His boss at the time was quick to describe Asmerom G. as talented, reliable, and "capable of anything," according to Bild newspaper.

However, then trouble began. Within a year, Asmerom G. was in trouble with the law. A brawl led to a conviction for grievous bodily harm at Siegburg District Court, earning him a six-month suspended sentence.

He moved on from Rheinbach and took up work behind the wheel of a freight truck. Somewhere along the way, he made a trip back to his home country - for reasons that remain unclear - and returned to Germany with a woman named Weghata A., who was 31 at the time, his wife under Eritrean law. On July 26, 2025, she delivered their daughter.

The child is now in the care of authorities. Lawyer Gesine Ickert, representing the daughter and the deceased's father, has stated that the child is well looked after under the circumstances.

The trial continues.

title: Legendary Swiss Bank "Thinks The Unthinkable"; Report
desc:
Legendary Swiss Bank "Thinks The Unthinkable"; Report

Swiss banking giant UBS is considering abandoning its home country and relocating to the United States as a bitter battle over government regulations threatens to upend one of the world's most powerful financial institutions.

The Zurich-based banking powerhouse and its advisers have drawn up contingency plans to move its headquarters abroad if Swiss lawmakers impose sweeping new capital requirements, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The bank has also received approaches from potential American deal partners, although no negotiations are underway and no formal steps toward a transaction have been taken.

Such a move would mark a stunning rupture between Switzerland and a financial institution synonymous with the country's centuries-old reputation as a global banking haven.

Among the options reportedly under consideration are acquiring a U.S. financial institution and redomiciling, merging with a European rival or selling UBS to an American banking giant.

The escalating confrontation traces back to the spectacular 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse, which forced UBS to absorb its longtime rival in a government-backed emergency rescue.

Last month, Switzerland's upper house of parliament backed a proposal requiring UBS to support its foreign subsidiaries with 90% common equity tier 1 capital.

UBS estimates the measure would force it to hold roughly $16 billion in additional capital, phased in over seven years.

The proposal still requires approval from parliament's lower house, where it could be watered down, and a final decision is not expected before next year.

An earlier government proposal was even more aggressive, with UBS estimating it would have required approximately $24 billion in additional capital.

UBS has fiercely resisted the measures, warning that the requirements would leave it at a severe competitive disadvantage against American and European rivals.

The regulatory battle has also sparked a backlash from major shareholders.

Investment firm Artisan Partners, which manages more than 60 million UBS shares, urged the bank's board in an October 1 letter to abandon Switzerland, blasting the proposed regulations as "punitive" and arguing there was no compelling reason to remain a Swiss company.

Activist investor Cevian Capital has similarly warned that the reforms would make it "not viable" to operate a global bank from Switzerland.

The threat of a dramatic departure has been building for months.

UBS was first reported to be exploring a potential relocation in early 2025, while Chairman Colm Kelleher later held private discussions with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent about what moving the bank's legal home to America might entail.

Losing UBS could deal a devastating blow to Switzerland's status as one of the world's premier financial centers.

The bank holds roughly $1.7 trillion in assets, equivalent to approximately 150% of Switzerland's entire economic output.

However, Swiss officials are no showing any signs of backing down.

Swiss Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter dismissed the relocation threat, warning that abandoning the country would be "far more expensive and legally complex" than complying with the proposed regulations.

"It would also cease to be a Swiss bank," she said in an interview with Schweiz am Wochenende, arguing that UBS's business model depends on Switzerland's legal system and political stability.

"UBS certainly doesn't have to leave Switzerland. Many analysts and specialists agree that the requirements are reasonable and easily manageable for UBS," she added. "The capital inflows experienced by private banks during the conflicts in the Middle East clearly demonstrate the confidence in Switzerland as a business location."

Swiss National Bank President Martin Schlegel echoed those concerns.

"Ultimately, the choice of headquarters is a decision for UBS," Schlegel told public broadcaster SRF. "Of course, it's a large bank and brings benefits to Switzerland. But Switzerland, of course, also brings benefits to UBS."

No final decision has been made, and UBS could ultimately choose to remain in Switzerland.

title: People in the US: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?
desc:
We’d like to hear about whether you feel like the US is in a recession and what you think signals such a downturn

Nearly two-thirds of Americans think the US is experiencing a recession, according to a new Harris Poll conducted for the Guardian. By the typical definition of a recession – when a country’s economic growth is in the negative for two consecutive quarters – the US is not experiencing one. Still, Americans are facing higher prices and a stagnant job market, which for many feels like a downturn.

We want to hear from Americans: do you feel like the US is experiencing a recession? title: Record Tanker Rates Leave Heavy Crude Stranded In The Americas
desc:
Record Tanker Rates Leave Heavy Crude Stranded In The Americas

Authored by Irina Slav via OilPrice.com,

  • Record tanker rates are creating a heavy crude glut in the Americas, pushing Canadian, Colombian, and Ecuadorian crude prices down roughly $10 per barrel.

  • Shipping costs have surged to $40 per barrel, making American heavy crude increasingly uneconomical for Asian and European refiners.

  • The global diesel crunch is set to persist, as tanker shortages prevent heavy crude from reaching markets where demand remains strong.

The Middle East crisis has driven tanker rates to all-time highs and created a shortage of vessels. This oil logistics problem is now causing a ripple effect, tipping the heavy crude market in North and South America into oversupply - while Asia and Europe grapple with a shortage of heavy grades.

Canada is producing over 5 million barrels of crude daily, most of it heavy crude. Some 4 million barrels daily of that goes south to U.S. refineries. Venezuelan production has also moved higher after the U.S. disposed of the country's government and took control of the oil industry. According to Reuters, a lot of this heavy crude is stuck at home because of the record freight costs that have dampened appetite, pressuring prices in Canada, Colombia, and Ecuador. Venezuelan crude goes mostly to the U.S. Gulf Coast, so it is not as vulnerable to freight rate developments.

Prices for Canadian, Colombia, and Ecuadorian heavy crude have all shed some $10 per barrel in recent weeks, the report said, citing Argus data. All the flagship grades are now trading at the lowest in six weeks, with Western Canadian Select reaching $74 per barrel last week, before rebounding to $79.50 at the time of writing.

Ecuador's flagship heavy crude grade, Oriente, has also recovered, after dropping to $76 per barrel last week, now trading at over 84 per barrel. Colombia's Vasconia was the most expensive of the three last week, trading at $84 per barrel, and it has also probably gone up this week, as all oil gains on the flurry of tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

These prices cited above seem quite enticing on a market where Russian Urals fetches close to $120 per barrel, and Iran Light sells for $104 per barrel, despite the U.S. Navy blockade. However, these prices exclude freight costs and insurance, and these have reached up to $40 per barrel of crude, at a time when heavy crude is in especially strong demand because of the global diesel crunch. Heavy crude yields more diesel than lighter grades, which is quite a hot topic right now.

"You need a ship and the price of ships are going up, and the availability ships are going down," TP ICAP analyst Scott Shelton told Reuters. Global tanker rates have soared this year due to Middle Eastern producers taking to ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz. For this, they use shuttle tankers, including smaller carriers, to sneak the oil through Hormuz and then load it on supertankers in the Gulf of Oman. As a result, supertanker rates from the Gulf to Asia hit $1.4 million daily earlier this month.

Shipping costs on the route from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Europe, meanwhile, have surged to $46 million in total, equal to $24.50 per barrel of crude. That compares to $6.5 million, or some $4 per barrel, before the war. The price is even higher on the route from the Americas to Asia, at over $80 million or $40 per barrel. It is little wonder why refiners in Europe and Asia are balking at the price and staying away from purchases.

This combination of factors suggests that the diesel crunch is not about to go away anytime soon. With heavy crude barrels stuck in the Americas because of freight costs, and few alternative suppliers of the same scale as Canada, for example, the market imbalance appears set to stay for a while. As long as there are so many vessels tied up in ship-to-ship transfers, freight costs are unlikely to move down meaningfully enough to stimulate cross-Atlantic demand for more heavy crude.

Tyler Durden Fri, 10/16/2026 - 05:00

title: Greta At French School Riot: "Our Future Is Being Robbed From Us"
desc:
Greta At French School Riot: "Our Future Is Being Robbed From Us"

Greta Thunberg joined high-school students outside the Paul Éluard lycée in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, on Tuesday, applauding hundreds of teenagers protesting run-down schools, the Associated Press reported. Staff and students at the school have long complained of dilapidated buildings and rat infestations, AP said.

The Interior Ministry put Tuesday's turnout at 161,500 nationwide, 41,500 of them in Paris. AP also reported that a 15-year-old lost a hand during the unrest and that the interior minister has suspended one type of police stun grenade. The riots have spread to Belgium, as ZH has reported, and Spiked counts more than 6,800 arrests.

Thunberg told reporters outside the school: "Whether it's not funding schools enough, or the climate crisis, or the social-injustice crises... Our future is being robbed from us."

As Spiked's Hugo Timms notes further, Thunberg's self-pity and vanity have been on show in the various prequels to Greta in Paris. Last October, she led the Global Salmud Flotilla from Europe to Palestine, in what she claimed to be an attempt to deliver aid to Gazans. Yet when her woke armada was intercepted by the Israeli navy, the authorities claimed there was no food or medical supplies on any of the ships. And when Thunberg and her fellow activists were detained and swiftly deported, they accused the Israelis of 'kidnapping' them. Speaking at a press conference in Athens, Greta told reporters, 'I could talk for a very, very long time about our mistreatment and abuses, trust me', although she refused to elaborate on any specifics. It was hard to discern whose alleged suffering she was most perturbed by - that of the Gazans or her own.

Indeed, a sense of her personal suffering has been front and centre of the Thunberg cult from the very beginning. When Greta began skipping school to protest against climate change (remember that?) in late 2018, her own feelings were front and centre: 'I want to feel safe. How can I feel safe when I know we are in the greatest crisis in human history?' Then came the apocalyptic deluge she dumped on the UN in 2019: 'You have stolen my dreams and my childhood... How dare you!' She didn't quite stamp her feet, although the then 16-year-old did let the audience know that she was 'sad and angry' with them. 'I shouldn't be up here. I should be back in school, on the other side of the ocean.'

And yet here Greta is, all grown up, from skipping school over wildfires to fanning the flames of a protest movement that's burning schools to the ground. The omnicause has truly come full circle.

Hugo Timms is a staff writer at spiked.

title: NATO's "Theory Of Victory" Isn't Anything New
desc:
NATO's "Theory Of Victory" Isn't Anything New

Authored by Andrew Korybko via Substack,

As the saying goes, “the more things change, the more they stay in the same.”

US General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's top commander, shared the bloc's long-awaited "Theory of Victory" during his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum. In his words, "should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then, if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us." He then elaborated that conventional forces would block an initial attack, unmanned ones would blunt any continued invasion, and precision strikes would break the adversary's warfighting system.

This isn't anything new since it's been considered the non-nuclear way of waging war between nuclear powers since the dawn of the drone age ushered in by the Ukrainian Conflict nearly half a decade ago. A nuclear power will likely only resort to such arms if they're completely overwhelmed in the first phase or their warfighting system is ultimately broken. Recently, "Russia Made It Clear That Nuclear War Would Follow Any Serious Aggression Against Kaliningrad", which is difficult to conventionally defend.

The same doesn't hold true for any part of NATO, not even the Baltic States, which are all connected to one another unlike Russia's Kaliningrad exclave. Even in the political fantasy of Russia invading the "Suwałki Corridor/Gap", counteroffensives could still be carried out from the Baltic States, Kaliningrad remains exposed, and Norway and Finland could open up a northern front. Reflecting on this, "The EU Poses A Much More Credible Threat To Russia Than The Inverse", which has always been the reality.

Although Grynkewich claimed that NATO's "Theory of Victory" is purely defensive and being publicly revealed for deterrence purposes, that's unlikely to assuage Russia, which reasonably considers the bloc's continued eastward expansion - especially its de facto expansion into Ukraine - to constitute a threat. Accordingly, its medium-term defense strategy will likely seek to thwart the scenario of NATO's "Theory of Victory" being exploited for offensive purposes, thus entailing a three-part counterplan.

Just like the Baltic States and Poland are building what's known as the "European Defense Line" along their borders with Russia and Belarus, so too could they build symmetrical infrastructure to impede any conventional offensive. As for the second phase's drone dimension, they could replicate the EU's planned "drone wall", which will include both offensive and defensive (interceptor) drones. And finally, more air defenses can thwart strikes against their warfighting systems, but they must be scaled nationwide.

As the saying goes, "the more things change, the more they stay in the same." In this case, the fundamental logic of a non-nuclear war between NATO and Russia remains the same, namely that each would rely on a combination of conventional forces, unmanned ones, and long-range precision strikes. Nukes would likely only be resorted to in the event that they overwhelm the other or ultimately break their warfighting systems, but that could happen quite quickly, perhaps as soon as the first hour.

What's urgently needed to prevent the worst-case scenario of World War III by miscalculation is mutual de-escalation between European NATO and Russia, especially along the "European Defense Line" that constitutes the bulk of NATO's Eastern Flank, which Trump could help mediate. As proposed here, the first step could be a crisis-control channel between the US, Poland, and Russia followed by mutual military pullbacks, which could set the basis for stabilizing the post-war European security architecture.

title: Starlink Antennas Set Ablaze By Masked Intruders Near Bulgarian Capital
desc:
Starlink Antennas Set Ablaze By Masked Intruders Near Bulgarian Capital

SpaceX operations in Eastern Europe have been in the news a lot lately, especially after Ukraine's President Zelensky very publicly accused Elon Musk's company of throttling access in Ukraine, which impacted the military's front line operations.

But something else happened simultaneous to the controversy over Ukraine this week in Bulgaria which has gone largely under-reported. Unknown masked intruders broke into a communications facility near the capital Sofia and destroyed 11 of its 17 antennas used to communicate with Starlink satellite.

The sabotage incident was revealed by Bulgarian National Television. Bulgarian lawmaker Ivaylo Mirchev has also highlighted the incident, posting video of the fire at the communications site.

"Clearly, these antennas were deliberately targeted, since they provide the main connection to the satellites," Mirchev said, while also pointing the finger at Russian intelligence, though without providing evidence.

Amid the emerging reports, it remains unknown or unconfirmed whether the damaged antennas were actually part of any network of communications connected to Ukraine's military.

Something similar was reported as happening in nearby Poland earlier this week:

Following a fire at a strategic facility in Poland crucial for maintaining internet connections in neighboring Ukraine, German police detained four people. Authorities in Warsaw suspect it was an act of sabotage orchestrated by Russia. Following a fire at a Starlink station in central Poland, German law enforcement officers detained several suspects.

Two Turkish citizens were apprehended and are being charged with setting fire to the building.

At this point, tensions between NATO and Moscow are so high that pretty much any fire at a sensitive facility in Europe - especially in Eastern Europe or the Baltic region - gets treated as a suspected Russian sabotage attack.

Some reports are assuming the sabotage is likely related to the Starlink systems outage suffered in Ukraine this week...

Bulgarian MP Ivaylo Mirchev said two masked individuals deliberately set fire to 11 of 17 Starlink antennas at a secret facility near Sofia. The antennas reportedly support satellite communications used in Ukraine’s war effort. Bulgarian authorities confirmed an investigation is underway and said security at similar facilities has been tightened.

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 14, 2026

At the same time, drone incursions have also become a monthly thing, and NATO leadership is broadly alleging that the Kremlin is conducting a well-coordinated hybrid campaign.

MS NOW Retracts Report That FBI Director Kash Patel Landed In Russia
desc:
MS NOW Retracts Report That FBI Director Kash Patel Landed In Russia

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

MS NOW has retracted a report that FBI Director Kash Patel landed in Russia on Oct. 14.

"We regret this error," Ken Dilanian, an MS Now reporter, said on air during an afternoon show.

MS Now host Peter Alexander had said during a broadcast on Wednesday morning that he had breaking news to report - that Patel "has landed in Russia for a meeting scheduled to take place there." He attributed the reporting to two anonymous sources, or two people "familiar with the matter."

The FBI responded by posting a video of Patel at an event at Liberty University in Virginia. Members of Congress, including Rep. John McGuire (R-Va.), also shared photographs of themselves with Patel at the event.

"MS Now's 'sources' are 'familiar' with NOTHING!" the FBI said in a post on X.

Ben Williamson, an FBI spokesman, wrote in another post on the social media platform: "I have had many strange experiences in life, but in tier 1 had to be seeing a clip of MS Now reporting breaking news that Kash Patel has 'just landed in Russia' - right as I'm receiving pics of Kash Patel doing a law enforcement appreciation event today in Lynchburg, Virginia."

Dilanian said during a show hosted by Alicia Menendez later Wednesday that the network had "since learned that Patel did not, in fact, land in Russia today and remains in the U.S."

After saying the FBI had not answered MS Now's questions about the purported trip, Dilanian referenced reports alleging Patel has a planned meeting in Russia and added that some Democrats have told Patel not to attend.

"But we do know now that he has not already landed in Russia, as we reported earlier. The timing of any potential trip remains unclear," Dilanian said. "Again, we regret this error, and we are transparent about when we make errors."

The Society of Professional Journalists recommends that outlets identify sources whenever feasible and, if using unnamed sources, include as much information as possible without revealing details that could lead to them being identified.

MS Now did not respond to questions, including whether it plans to work with the same sources moving forward, by the time of publication.

MS Now removed a video that featured a former FBI agent commenting on the report. The former agent had called Patel a "babe in the woods" when it came to Russia. It also posted Dilanian's apology on its website.

"This reporting has been updated in keeping with our policy of transparency, including promptly correcting any errors," the outlet said.

President Donald Trump recently banned MS Now and several other outlets from the White House, saying they consistently reported fake news. A federal judge blocked the ban as the outlets' legal case against it proceeds. The government has appealed the block.

Patel, following the correction, wrote in an Oct. 14 post on X, "From Russia, with Love..."

He also said MS Now "constantly tells lies about this FBI and law enforcement's historic achievements in safeguarding the American people."

title: The problem with living in a rich man’s world | Letters
desc:
David Redshaw and Fernando Quintana respond to reports of a billionaire exodus from Britain

The idea that the departure of the super-rich is a problem ignores a historical fact (Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground, 7 October). Capitalism works better without them. The most successful countries today are states where redistributive taxation has empowered the working masses and provided a better and more stable market for business people.

title: Nearly Half Of Muslims & Jews Consider Leaving France If Le Pen Wins; New Poll Finds
desc:
Nearly Half Of Muslims & Jews Consider Leaving France If Le Pen Wins; New Poll Finds

Authored by - Remix News Staff - via Remix News,

Nearly half of Muslim and Jewish respondents in a major French poll say they would consider leaving the country if Marine Le Pen wins the 2027 presidential election, according to an exclusive Ifop survey for the magazine Marianne.

The poll found that 46 percent of respondents identifying as Muslim would contemplate "leaving France to settle in another country" under a Le Pen presidency. Of those, 20 percent said they would "certainly" take that step. By comparison, 21 percent of the overall population expressed a similar willingness to leave.

The figure is part of a broader set of findings on identity, secularism, and anticipated reactions to a National Rally (RN) victory. Eighty-one percent of Muslim respondents believed a Le Pen win would lead to a rise in discrimination against their community. Twenty-seven percent said they would consider concealing their religious identity in daily life, including 18 percent who would stop wearing the veil in public.

Similar sentiments appeared in other groups polled.

Forty percent of the youngest cohort of French voters, 43 percent of France Unbowed (LFI) voters, and 44 percent of Jewish respondents said they would consider leaving. The survey also recorded elevated support for civil disobedience in some cohorts. For instance, substantial shares indicated they would refuse to respect laws they viewed as unjust.

Notably, while Le Pen has been antagonistic towards Islam in France, she has often cast herself as a protector of Jewish life in the country.

In 2024, she said, "The best shield for French people of the Jewish faith is the National Rally. It is the only movement that has the will, the conviction and the means to fight Islamist fundamentalism, which is the major danger facing them."

Yet, nearly as many Jews said they would leave the country as Muslims.

Le meilleur bouclier pour les Français de confession juive, c'est le Rassemblement National.

C'est le seul mouvement qui a la volonté, la conviction et les moyens de lutter contre le fondamentalisme islamiste qui est le danger majeur qui pèse sur eux. https://t.co/pggWHgzITu

— Marine Le Pen (@MLP_officiel) May 6, 2024

François Kraus, director of the Politics and Current Affairs division at Ifop, described the results: "The arrival in power of the candidate favored by the polls risks creating significant obstacles and generates high levels of fear and a sense of insecurity."

The National Rally has long advocated tighter controls on immigration, greater priority for French nationals in housing and employment, and restrictions on Islamic veiling in public spaces. Le Pen has indicated she would not impose an immediate ban on the veil upon taking office but would put broader restrictions to a national referendum.

Previous Ifop work has documented rising religiosity and support for more rigorous interpretations of Islam among younger French Muslims, including significant shares prioritizing Islamic norms over French civil law on issues such as inheritance or ritual slaughter in certain scenarios. Remix News reported on this poll last year.

Figures on the right treated these results as evidence of failed integration and the dangers of demographic change.

Currently, Le Pen has frequently led first-round voting intention polls, making her the favorite to win the presidential election.

It is important to note that many groups claim they will leave a country if their preferred candidate does not win an election, but actually leaving is an entirely different story. The 46 percent figure for Muslims and 44 percent for Jews is only an expressed willingness or contemplation in a hypothetical scenario, not concrete plans to leave France.

The reality is that family ties, employment, and economic realities mean that leaving is far harder in practice.
